newsitem.title: USA: American, its pilots, resume labor talks.
newsitem.headline: American, its pilots, resume labor talks.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots union resumed contract talks Wednesday, hoping to reach a settlement on pay and a dispute over which pilots will fly new commuter jets American plans to buy.

The Washington negotiations followed "productive" talks at a resort near Seattle over the weekend that were overseen by Robert Harris, chairman of the Presidential Emergency Board that was formed after earlier talks collapsed and the pilots went on strike.

At issue between the nation's No. 2 airline and the Allied Pilots Association are a pay raise for 9,300 pilots and whether the union's pilots will fly new, small jets American plans to buy for its American Eagle commuter airline or whether Eagle pilots will fly them. Eagle pilots are represented by another union.
American said Tuesday it expected a tentative agreement could be reached by Friday, when the Allied Pilots Association's board of directors is scheduled to meet in Washington.
Union President James Sovich said he expected bargaining would continue until Friday, when any progress would be reported to the board.

The board could accept an agreement and send it to its members for a vote, or reject it. The panel recommended a tentative accord reached last summer, but 61 percent of the union's members voted it down.
Union spokesman Michael Cronin said the latest talks were not being held face to face, because some union negotiators were not yet here, but by fax and telephone conference call.

The PEB's recommedations for a settlement were to be sent to President Clinton later on Wednesday. But Cronin said that with the talks continuing, the recommendations may or not be part of any settlement.
Clinton created the board on Feb. 15, minutes after five days of round-the-clock talks between American and the union broke down and the pilots went out on strike.

Under terms of the law invoked to create the PEB, the pilots were required to go back to work for 30 days while the board fashioned a proposed settlement and remain on the job for another 30 while the two sides considered whether or not to accept it.
The "cooling off" period has been extended to April 28, when the union will be free to strike.
Then, only Congress could end a strike, by passing legislation to send the pilots back to work and to require them to accept the PEB's recommended settlement or to accept binding arbitration.

At issue in the dispute is a difference of 4.5 percent in pay. The pilots want a pay increase of 11 percent to cover the past three years, when they had no increase, and the next four. American has offered 6.5 percent.
The APA wants its pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, to fly the new commuter jets, but American wants them flown by Eagle pilots, who earn about $35,000.
